name: Nora Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Nora, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, how would you describe your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Daniel and I run Hollow Oak, his family's farm up the lane from the chapel. It's 120 beef cattle, hay and oats, and a few pigs for the freezer. His parents still own the land and live in the old house; we built our own place on the corner field twelve years back, and that's where the mortgage is. I've worked this farm twenty years, since before we married.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five, kettle on, then out to feed and bed the cattle and check the water troughs, which freeze in winter and need a hammer. Mornings I do the cattle and the paperwork by hand in the big ledger, Daniel does the fieldwork and the machinery. Afternoons it's hay in the summer, fencing in the winter, and picking up Rosa and Mateo from school. I love it when the calves are out in spring and the whole valley's green. What wears me out is the forms and people telling me I need an app for this and that, which I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said, people got carried away with a gadget. We'd talk about it after chapel and have a laugh. I don't go online much, just the weather and the market prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means we carry on as we are, and that suits me fine. The farm's been in Daniel's family four generations and it's done all right without a computer brain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always. Feed the cattle, cut the hay, put a bit by each month. We've a good bit saved already and Daniel's parents have the land, so we're steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad, really. It's one less thing to fret about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep the farm records in a ledger. Has anyone pushed you to change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young lad from the feed merchant keeps telling me to put it all on his tablet. I tell him the ledger never runs out of battery. Daniel's mother kept it the same way and her numbers were never wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rosa and Mateo about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That hard work and good neighbours count for more than any machine. They know that already, mind. Mateo's more interested in tractors than phones, thank goodness.

S0.say: I'd say people got carried away with a gadget, and we'd have a laugh about it after chapel. I don't go online much beyond the weather and market prices.
S0.think: For me it means we carry on as we are, and that suits me fine. The farm has done all right for four generations without a computer brain.
S0.do: Keeps feeding the cattle, making hay and saving a bit each month. Keeps the farm records in the paper ledger as before.
S0.feel: Calm and glad there's one less thing to fret about.
S0.quote: I tell him the ledger never runs out of battery.
S0.fieldNote: Nora is content with how things are and proud of doing things by hand. Her security comes from savings, family land and four generations of farming. She shows humour about the push for apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a lot of change and not all of it's good. Some of it'll be useful, I'm sure, but I'd want to see it working on someone else's farm first. I'd say that at chapel and to the neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it bothers me. I don't want to learn computers at my age. I worry the farm will need things I can't do, and I'll be the one holding Daniel back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing straight away. I'd wait and see, keep the farm going, and let Daniel decide on the machines, he's better with them. I'd keep putting money aside like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit like hearing a new noise in the engine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think pushes these changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies, the ones in the cities who've never seen a calf born. They sell the machines and the government lets them. I'm all for business, but it should serve the farm, not the other way round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the family consider taking on any new machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel might, if his dad agrees. A robot for the hay bales maybe. But not the cattle, I'd put my foot down. The cattle know my voice.

S1.say: I'd say there's a lot of change and not all of it good, and I'd want to see it working on someone else's farm first. I'd say that at chapel and to the neighbours.
S1.think: It bothers me, because I don't want to learn computers at my age. I worry I'll be the one holding Daniel back.
S1.do: Waits to see what changes and keeps the farm going as it is. Leaves machinery decisions to her husband and keeps saving as usual.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing a new noise in the engine.
S1.quote: But not the cattle, I'd put my foot down. The cattle know my voice.
S1.fieldNote: Nora's resistance is personal and protective, especially around the cattle. She blames distant companies and a government that lets them, but still says she's all for business. Her private worry is about holding her husband back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong and it's too fast, and the people pushing it don't care about families like ours. I'd say it in chapel and at the school gate. I might even go to a meeting in town, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm frightened. If a robot can run the cattle and the fields, what's left for us? The land's still ours, but what's the point of a farm with no farmers?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard: no holidays, no new car, the kids' riding lessons stop. I'd keep feeding the cattle myself as long as we can. And I'd lean on the chapel and on Daniel's family to get through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not sleep. I'd be up at the window looking at the dark yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very little time. What does that do to the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and nobody's ready. No time to think, no time to pray on it. Just a rush, and we'd be left standing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chapel first, they'd rally round, they always do. And Daniel's parents. Not the government, I don't want handouts, I want our work.

S2.say: I'd say it's wrong and too fast, and the people pushing it don't care about families like ours. I'd say it at chapel, at the school gate and maybe at a meeting in town.
S2.think: I'm frightened, because if a robot can run the cattle and fields, what's left for us? The land's still ours, but what's the point of a farm with no farmers?
S2.do: Cuts holidays, a new car and the children's riding lessons. Keeps feeding the cattle herself and leans on the chapel and her husband's family rather than the government.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, staring at the dark yard at night.
S2.quote: The land's still ours, but what's the point of a farm with no farmers?
S2.fieldNote: Nora's fear is about purpose, not money: the land and savings are safe, but the work is gone. She would turn to chapel and family rather than government help. She'd even go to a public meeting, which shows how strong this would hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still too fast, but at least we can see it coming. I'd tell the neighbours to get ready, to stick together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think we'd lose the farm work, but we'd keep the land and the family. That's what matters. Five years is enough time to make sure of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, pay down the house, maybe sell a bit of cattle at the top of the market. I'd talk to Rosa and Mateo about apprenticeships, something with their hands that a robot can't do. I'd keep the cattle going as long as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A dull ache, not a sharp one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade they can be proud of. Rosa likes baking, maybe she could run a bakery. Mateo wants to be a mechanic. Something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Rosa and Mateo in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years to settle things. Pay off the house, have money for the kids. And keep going to chapel. That doesn't change.

S3.say: I'd say it's still too fast, but at least we can see it coming. I'd tell the neighbours to get ready and stick together.
S3.think: I think we'd lose the farm work but keep the land and the family, and that's what matters. Five years is enough to make sure of that.
S3.do: Saves harder, pays down the house and sells some cattle at the top of the market. Talks with her children about apprenticeships and keeps the cattle going as long as she can.
S3.feel: Anxious, a dull ache rather than a sharp one.
S3.quote: Rosa likes baking, maybe she could run a bakery. Mateo wants to be a mechanic. Something real.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Nora's fear into steady preparation centred on family. She favours apprenticeships and hands-on trades for her children. She still won't learn new tech herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's do it right. Look after families, keep the farms with the people who know them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is just longer to dread it. I'd be 53, the kids grown or nearly. I'd still be losing the life I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much differently, if I'm honest. Save, pay down the house, keep the farm. Help the kids find a trade. I'm not going to learn computers, so there's no point pretending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still. Like waiting for the vet's news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Does that change how it feels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. It's still the same end. I'd just have more time to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd start now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd start teaching Rosa and Mateo everything I know about the cattle, so it's not lost. Even if they never farm, they'll know.

S4.say: I'd say there's time, so let's do it right. We should look after families and keep the farms with the people who know them.
S4.think: Ten years is just longer to dread it. I'd be 53 with the kids nearly grown, and still losing the life I know.
S4.do: Keeps saving, paying down the house and running the farm. Helps the children find a trade and starts teaching them everything she knows about the cattle.
S4.feel: Still anxious, like waiting for the vet's news.
S4.quote: Honestly, ten years is just longer to dread it.
S4.fieldNote: For Nora, more time does not ease the fear, because she won't change and the end is the same. She'd use the time to pass on knowledge to her children. Her calm public line hides real dread.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to settle things or pray on it. What would help is keeping farms with families, not with the big companies, and helping people find work with their hands, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. I'd lean on God and my chapel through all of it. Whatever comes, that doesn't change.

headlineQuote: Not the government, I don't want handouts, I want our work.
portrait: Nora Garcia is a 43-year-old farmer who runs Hollow Oak, her husband's family's beef, hay and oat farm, with two children and a strong chapel community. She keeps the records in a paper ledger and refuses new tech, though she leaves machinery choices to her husband. She is calm if AI stalls and uneasy with steady change. Fast AGI alarms her because it takes the purpose out of farming, and longer timelines only stretch the dread. She leans on family and faith, not government, and wants her children in hands-on trades.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time to settle things or pray on it.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping farms in family hands rather than big companies, and helping people find hands-on work instead of handouts.
